- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next period.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.50), model often underestimates; adjust upward by 1–2% to counteract pessimism.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots in the following 3–5 days; apply a 1–3% downward correction.
- If model shows strong mean reversion bias (e.g., forecasting back to historical mean after volatility), check if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive — if so, allow slight overcorrection to avoid missing upward momentum.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows persistent downward trend (e.g., 3 consecutive drops >1%), model often fails to recognize it; apply a 1–2% downward bias to early periods.
- If sentiment history shows alternating highs/lows (e.g., 1–2 positive, 1–2 negative), model tends to overreact to sentiment swings; dampen forecast volatility by 10–20% in the next 5–7 days.
- When sentiment is flat or neutral (0.33–0.67), model often underperforms; increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% to account for hidden market resilience.
